note.note:
History:
• 28-year-old woman with first-ever headache that began yesterday mid-morning  
• Location: left posterior (occipital) region  
• Quality/severity: intense, throbbing; rates pain 8/10; gradual build-up, then persistent  
• No clear diurnal, positional, coughing/sneezing or activity-related change  
• Associated symptoms denied: nausea, vomiting, visual changes, photophobia, phonophobia, tingling, numbness, weakness, fever, chills, sweats, rash, neck stiffness  
• Appetite, hydration and overnight sleep normal; able to work but with difficulty  
• Took single dose of ibuprofen (Nurofen) yesterday with minimal relief  
• No previous similar headaches or other neurologic episodes

Past Medical History:
• No chronic illnesses reported  
• Medications: none routinely; ibuprofen yesterday (dose/route/frequency not documented)  
• Allergies: none reported  
• Family history: mother with hypertension and migraines  
• Social: lives with partner; occupation—designer; non-smoker; no alcohol or recreational drug use; no recent travel or trauma

Physical Examination:
• Telehealth visit—no hands-on exam performed  
• Patient appears alert and oriented (via video)  
• Reports no focal neurologic deficits, no visual disturbances, no meningeal signs, no rash  
• Vital signs: not recorded

Impression:
New-onset unilateral throbbing headache without red-flag features; likely primary headache disorder.  
Top considerations (consistent with transcript):  
1. Migraine without aura – unilateral throbbing pain, functional impairment, positive family history.  
2. Tension-type headache – common primary headache; absence of associated migraine features.

Management Plan:
• Initiate alternative NSAID (specific drug/dose/route/frequency not documented) to be taken regularly with food, in place of ibuprofen  
• Add paracetamol (dose/route/frequency not documented) for additional analgesia  
• Advise rest and adequate hydration  
• Education on red-flag symptoms: worsening pain, persistent or recurrent attacks, fever, rash, vomiting, neck stiffness, focal neurologic changes—seek urgent review if these occur  
• Follow-up: patient to call back if headache not settling within 1–2 days after starting advised medication or if any red-flag symptoms develop

Patient Summary:
28-year-old woman with a 1-day history of new, severe left occipital throbbing headache. No associated systemic or neurologic signs. Clinical picture most consistent with a primary headache (probable migraine). Treated conservatively with alternative NSAID, paracetamol, rest, fluids, and close follow-up.

Key Takeaways:
• Start the prescribed stronger pain reliever instead of ibuprofen; may take paracetamol alongside.  
• Maintain good hydration and rest.  
• Seek prompt medical attention if headache worsens, lasts >48 h, or any new symptoms such as fever, rash, vomiting, stiff neck, or neurologic changes appear.

Next Steps:
• Re-assessment via telehealth or in-person if no improvement in 1–2 days.  
• Consider in-office evaluation with blood pressure measurement and focused neurologic exam if headaches persist or recur.  
• Escalate to imaging or specialty referral if red-flag features emerge.
